items.stem: Which of the following is the first principle listed in the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility (2012)?
items.answer: Do no harm
items.markingKey: C. The AAA statement begins with "Do No Harm".

items.stem: Distinguish between anonymity and confidentiality.
items.answer: Anonymity means the identity of participants is hidden in the research output; confidentiality means information shared with the researcher is not passed on beyond agreed limits. A participant can be anonymised yet information can still breach confidentiality if shared improperly.
items.markingKey: Anonymity means the identity of participants is hidden in the research output; confidentiality means information shared with the researcher is not passed on beyond agreed limits. A participant can be anonymised yet information can still breach confidentiality if shared improperly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why informed consent in anthropology is described as a process.
items.answer: Fieldwork is long and open-ended; research questions change, new people become involved and relationships deepen, so consent must be revisited and participants must be able to withdraw at any time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fieldwork is long and open-ended; research questions change, new people become involved and relationships deepen, so consent must be revisited and participants must be able to withdraw at any time. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Once a participant signs a consent form, the anthropologist has no further ethical obligations." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Consent is ongoing; researchers must protect participants from harm, maintain confidentiality, allow withdrawal and consider the effects of publication long after consent is given.
items.markingKey: Consent is ongoing; researchers must protect participants from harm, maintain confidentiality, allow withdrawal and consider the effects of publication long after consent is given. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how social relations shapes the ethical conduct of fieldwork, using evidence from Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People.
items.answer: The controversy after Patrick Tierney's Darkness in El Dorado (2000) raised questions about gifts of steel tools, consent to the 1960s blood sampling, and the anthropologist's effect on relations between villages.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The controversy after Patrick Tierney's Darkness in El Dorado (2000) raised questions about gifts of steel tools, consent to the 1960s blood sampling, and the anthropologist's effect on relations between villages. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Napoleon Chagnon, Yanomamö: The Fierce People (1968), among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Havasupai blood-samples case (settled 2010) and explain what it reveals about the limits of informed consent.
items.answer: Blood samples given by members of the Havasupai Tribe in Arizona for diabetes research were later used without consent for studies of schizophrenia, inbreeding and migration origins; Arizona State University settled, paying compensation and returning samples. It shows that consent applies to specific uses; using data for purposes participants did not agree to – especially research contradicting their origin stories – causes real harm.
items.markingKey: Context (Blood samples given by members of the Havasupai Tribe in Arizona for diabetes research were later used without consent for studies of schizophrenia, inbreeding and migration origins; Arizona State University settled, paying compensation and returning samples.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows that consent applies to specific uses; using data for purposes participants did not agree to – especially research contradicting their origin stories – causes real harm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of informed consent.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Ethical codes such as the AAA principles are sufficient to guide anthropologists in the field."
items.answer: Codes are necessary guides but must be applied through reflexive judgement in context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they provide clear principles such as do no harm and informed consent; they are regularly revised (AAA 2012, ASA 2021). Arguments against: codes are general and fieldwork dilemmas are specific and unpredictable; local ideas of consent and harm may differ; codes cannot resolve conflicts between obligations. Supported judgement: Codes are necessary guides but must be applied through reflexive judgement in context.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The headteacher agreed that I could observe classes at the girls' school and signed the permission letter. In the staffroom, though, Ms Haddad asked me not to write about her lessons: "If the inspectors read that I speak Arabic in the English class, I lose my job." Two pupils showed me a group chat where they share answers before tests and asked if I would "put it in the book". One of them added, laughing, "Use my real name, I want to be famous." When I returned the following term, a new headteacher knew nothing about my research.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a secondary school in Jordan.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: Do no harm: Ms Haddad's job and the pupils' academic standing could be damaged; minors require parental consent and their wish for fame does not override protection; anonymise the school; renegotiate access with the new headteacher; store chat screenshots securely or not at all. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Do no harm: Ms Haddad's job and the pupils' academic standing could be damaged; minors require parental consent and their wish for fame does not override protection; anonymise the school; renegotiate access with the new headteacher; store chat screenshots securely or not at all. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. items.stem: Explain why anonymity can be difficult to guarantee in ethnography.
items.answer: Ethnographies describe small communities in rich detail; even with pseudonyms, insiders can recognise people from roles, events or quotations, and online publication makes texts widely accessible.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ethnographies describe small communities in rich detail; even with pseudonyms, insiders can recognise people from roles, events or quotations, and online publication makes texts widely accessible. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists may owe obligations to more than one group.
items.answer: They have duties to participants, colleagues, funders, host governments and the public, which can conflict – e.g. a funder wants information that could harm participants – so the AAA asks them to weigh competing obligations, with participants' welfare first.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have duties to participants, colleagues, funders, host governments and the public, which can conflict – e.g. a funder wants information that could harm participants – so the AAA asks them to weigh competing obligations, with participants' welfare first. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between covert research and overt research.
items.answer: In overt research participants know they are being studied and can consent; in covert research they do not, which breaches informed consent and is justified only in exceptional cases such as exposing serious harm.
items.markingKey: In overt research participants know they are being studied and can consent; in covert research they do not, which breaches informed consent and is justified only in exceptional cases such as exposing serious harm. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Can an anthropologist ever fully understand another way of life?" With reference to Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping and the key concept of social relations, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies social relations explicitly and uses ethnography: Facing very high infant mortality, some mothers delayed emotional attachment to babies judged weak and let them die "without weeping" – a contested argument about how scarcity shapes maternal love. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Using Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People and Bourgois's In Search of Respect, compare the ways in which social relations is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People (among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964)): The controversy after Patrick Tierney's Darkness in El Dorado (2000) raised questions about gifts of steel tools, consent to the 1960s blood sampling, and the anthropologist's effect on relations between villages. Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): As women entered wage work while men lost status, gender relations were renegotiated, and Bourgois documents how this contributed to domestic conflict and violence. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reciprocity in fieldwork"?
options: The expectation that the anthropologist gives something back – time, help, gifts, payment, advocacy or shared results – in return for participants' time and knowledge
The return of human remains, sacred objects or cultural property from museums and collections to the communities from which they were taken
Edward Said's term (1978) for Western representations that portrayed "the Orient" as exotic, backward and unchanging, justifying domination
The possibility that research produced for one purpose may be used by others – such as militaries or corporations – for purposes that harm participants
items.answer: The expectation that the anthropologist gives something back – time, help, gifts, payment, advocacy or shared results – in return for participants' time and knowledge
items.markingKey: A. "reciprocity in fieldwork" is the expectation that the anthropologist gives something back – time, help, gifts, payment, advocacy or shared results – in return for participants' time and knowledge.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Giving gifts to participants is always ethical because it repays them." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Gifts can create dependence, inequality or conflict and can shape what people tell the researcher, so their form and effects must be considered.
items.markingKey: Gifts can create dependence, inequality or conflict and can shape what people tell the researcher, so their form and effects must be considered. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why representation is an ethical issue as well as a methodological one.
items.answer: How people are portrayed can affect how they are treated by states, media and outsiders: an image of a group as "fierce" or "deviant" can justify discrimination, land seizure or policing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: How people are portrayed can affect how they are treated by states, media and outsiders: an image of a group as "fierce" or "deviant" can justify discrimination, land seizure or policing. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every evening, Nadia brings me tea and asks about visas. She knows I have a British passport, and her son wants to study in London. At first I answered vaguely; then I helped him complete an online application. Since then, Nadia introduces me to neighbours as "the one who helps with papers", and three families have asked me for the same help. When I wrote about a dispute between Nadia and her brother over the family land, she asked to read my notes. I hesitated: her brother had told me his side in confidence.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood in Amman, Jordan, during research with Syrian refugee families.

Explain, with close reference to the text, how the anthropologist's help creates ethical dilemmas of reciprocity and power. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: Helping with the visa is a form of reciprocity but changes the anthropologist's role and status ("the one who helps with papers"), raises expectations that cannot be met for every family and may influence what people say. Nadia's request to read notes conflicts with the confidence of her brother, so obligations to different participants clash.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Helping with the visa is a form of reciprocity but changes the anthropologist's role and status ("the one who helps with papers"), raises expectations that cannot be met for every family and may influence what people say. Nadia's request to read notes conflicts with the confidence of her brother, so obligations to different participants clash. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Yanomami controversy following Darkness in El Dorado (2000) shows the ethics of representation and reciprocity.
items.answer: Critics accused Chagnon of portraying the Yanomami as "fierce" and of distributing steel goods that intensified conflict; Yanomami leaders later demanded the return of blood samples taken in the 1960s. It shows how gifts, consent and the image of a people in widely read texts can affect their relations and political position, and how communities now challenge researchers.
items.markingKey: Context (Critics accused Chagnon of portraying the Yanomami as "fierce" and of distributing steel goods that intensified conflict; Yanomami leaders later demanded the return of blood samples taken in the 1960s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows how gifts, consent and the image of a people in widely read texts can affect their relations and political position, and how communities now challenge researchers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the ethics of representation and reciprocity.

items.stem: Using Bourgois's In Search of Respect and Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People, compare the ways in which power is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People (among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964)): Critics argued that the portrayal of the Yanomami as "fierce" was used by gold miners and politicians to justify encroachment on Yanomami land. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Which US military programme (2007–2014) that embedded social scientists with combat units was condemned by the AAA Executive Board in 2007?
items.answer: The Human Terrain System
items.markingKey: B. The AAA argued it could not meet the requirements of informed consent and do no harm.

items.stem: Distinguish between reciprocity and payment.
items.answer: Reciprocity is a broad, relational obligation to give back in culturally appropriate ways (help, gifts, shared results); payment is a monetary transaction that may be fair but can turn participation into employment and influence what people say.
items.markingKey: Reciprocity is a broad, relational obligation to give back in culturally appropriate ways (help, gifts, shared results); payment is a monetary transaction that may be fair but can turn participation into employment and influence what people say. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Facing very high infant mortality, some mothers delayed emotional attachment to babies judged weak and let them die "without weeping" – a contested argument about how scarcity shapes maternal love.

items.stem: "Anthropologists have a duty to act as advocates for the people they study." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Anthropologists have a duty not to harm and often a responsibility to engage, but advocacy should be negotiated with participants and transparent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: researchers witness suffering and have a voice participants may lack (Scheper-Hughes, Farmer); neutrality in the face of injustice can be complicity. Arguments against: communities are divided, so whose interests are advocated?; advocacy may bias research or endanger participants; participants may not want an advocate. Supported judgement: Anthropologists have a duty not to harm and often a responsibility to engage, but advocacy should be negotiated with participants and transparent. Markbands (15 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Efforts to confront the discipline's colonial legacies by centring the knowledge, voices and control of formerly colonised and Indigenous peoples"?
items.answer: decolonising anthropology
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of decolonising anthropology.

items.stem: A student claims: "Colonialism is only a historical issue with no relevance to anthropology today." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Colonial legacies persist in museum collections, unequal research relations, global inequality and representations of formerly colonised peoples, so they shape current ethics.
items.markingKey: Colonial legacies persist in museum collections, unequal research relations, global inequality and representations of formerly colonised peoples, so they shape current ethics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between decolonising anthropology and salvage anthropology.
items.answer: Salvage anthropology recorded cultures believed to be vanishing, usually by outsiders for outside audiences; decolonising anthropology seeks to shift authority to the communities themselves and to analyse colonial power rather than freezing cultures in time.
items.markingKey: Salvage anthropology recorded cultures believed to be vanishing, usually by outsiders for outside audiences; decolonising anthropology seeks to shift authority to the communities themselves and to analyse colonial power rather than freezing cultures in time. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to the Benin Bronzes, explain how it illustrates colonial power and the ethics of representation.
items.answer: Thousands of brass and ivory works were looted from Benin City by a British punitive expedition in 1897 and dispersed to European museums; several institutions began returning them in the 2020s. Museum displays long presented the objects as "primitive art" divorced from the violence of their acquisition; repatriation debates show communities reclaiming control over their heritage.
items.markingKey: Context (Thousands of brass and ivory works were looted from Benin City by a British punitive expedition in 1897 and dispersed to European museums; several institutions began returning them in the 2020s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: museum displays long presented the objects as "primitive art" divorced from the violence of their acquisition; repatriation debates show communities reclaiming control over their heritage. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to colonial power and the ethics of representation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the museum's storeroom, the curator unwrapped a carved house post. The label from 1911 read: "Idol of a vanished tribe." Mere, an elder from the iwi that had travelled to view it, laid her hand on the wood and spoke to it for several minutes before speaking to us. "He is not vanished," she said. "He is our ancestor and we are here." The curator explained that the trustees would need a formal claim and provenance research. Mere's nephew filmed the encounter on his phone; later he posted it with the caption: "Visiting our tupuna in prison."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a European museum storeroom during a visit by a Māori delegation.

Explain, with close reference to the text, how the text reveals the colonial legacy of anthropological classification. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: The 1911 label reflects salvage anthropology and colonial classification (idol, vanished tribe), denying the iwi's continued existence; Mere's emic view classifies the post as a living ancestor; the curator's bureaucratic procedures show institutional power over heritage; the nephew's caption reframes the museum as a prison, contesting representation and asserting change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The 1911 label reflects salvage anthropology and colonial classification (idol, vanished tribe), denying the iwi's continued existence; Mere's emic view classifies the post as a living ancestor; the curator's bureaucratic procedures show institutional power over heritage; the nephew's caption reframes the museum as a prison, contesting representation and asserting change. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "decolonising anthropology".
items.answer: Efforts to confront the discipline's colonial legacies by centring the knowledge, voices and control of formerly colonised and Indigenous peoples
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: efforts to confront the discipline's colonial legacies by centring the knowledge, voices and control of formerly colonised and Indigenous peoples. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why anthropology has been described as "the child of colonialism".
items.answer: The discipline developed as European empires expanded: colonial administrations funded or used research, fieldwork depended on colonial access and security, and early theories (e.g. evolutionism) ranked colonised peoples as inferior.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The discipline developed as European empires expanded: colonial administrations funded or used research, fieldwork depended on colonial access and security, and early theories (e.g. evolutionism) ranked colonised peoples as inferior. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Once a participant signs a consent form, the anthropologist has no further ethical obligations." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Consent is ongoing; researchers must protect participants from harm, maintain confidentiality, allow withdrawal and consider the effects of publication long after consent is given.

items.stem: Explain the difference between decolonising anthropology and salvage anthropology.
items.answer: Salvage anthropology recorded cultures believed to be vanishing, usually by outsiders for outside audiences; decolonising anthropology seeks to shift authority to the communities themselves and to analyse colonial power rather than freezing cultures in time.
items.markingKey: Salvage anthropology recorded cultures believed to be vanishing, usually by outsiders for outside audiences; decolonising anthropology seeks to shift authority to the communities themselves and to analyse colonial power rather than freezing cultures in time. items.stem: Distinguish between confidentiality and anonymity.
items.answer: Anonymity means the identity of participants is hidden in the research output; confidentiality means information shared with the researcher is not passed on beyond agreed limits. A participant can be anonymised yet information can still breach confidentiality if shared improperly.

items.stem: Explain the difference between reciprocity and payment.
items.answer: Reciprocity is a broad, relational obligation to give back in culturally appropriate ways (help, gifts, shared results); payment is a monetary transaction that may be fair but can turn participation into employment and influence what people say.
items.markingKey: Reciprocity is a broad, relational obligation to give back in culturally appropriate ways (help, gifts, shared results); payment is a monetary transaction that may be fair but can turn participation into employment and influence what people say. items.stem: Explain the difference between Orientalism and cultural relativism.
items.answer: Orientalism represents others as exotic and inferior, serving domination; cultural relativism seeks to understand others in their own terms without ranking, although critics note relativism can also exoticise.

The headteacher agreed that I could observe classes at the girls' school and signed the permission letter. In the staffroom, though, Ms Haddad asked me not to write about her lessons: "If the inspectors read that I speak Arabic in the English class, I lose my job." Two pupils showed me a group chat where they share answers before tests and asked if I would "put it in the book". One of them added, laughing, "Use my real name, I want to be famous." When I returned the following term, a new headteacher knew nothing about my research.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a secondary school in Jordan.

Consent is ongoing and relational.

items.stem: Identify one way in which social relations matters in Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: As women entered wage work while men lost status, gender relations were renegotiated, and Bourgois documents how this contributed to domestic conflict and violence.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every evening, Nadia brings me tea and asks about visas. She knows I have a British passport, and her son wants to study in London. At first I answered vaguely; then I helped him complete an online application. Since then, Nadia introduces me to neighbours as "the one who helps with papers", and three families have asked me for the same help. When I wrote about a dispute between Nadia and her brother over the family land, she asked to read my notes. I hesitated: her brother had told me his side in confidence.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood in Amman, Jordan, during research with Syrian refugee families.

Compare and contrast how social relations is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Nancy Scheper-Hughes, Death without Weeping: The Violence of Everyday Life in Brazil (1992)). Refer to specific evidence from both the text and the ethnography.
items.answer: Text: Helping with the visa is a form of reciprocity but changes the anthropologist's role and status ("the one who helps with papers"), raises expectations that cannot be met for every family and may influence what people say. Nadia's request to read notes conflicts with the confidence of her brother, so obligations to different participants clash. Ethnography – Nancy Scheper-Hughes, Death without Weeping: The Violence of Everyday Life in Brazil (1992), among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s): Facing very high infant mortality, some mothers delayed emotional attachment to babies judged weak and let them die "without weeping" – a contested argument about how scarcity shapes maternal love. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Havasupai blood-samples case (settled 2010) shows the limits of informed consent.
items.answer: Blood samples given by members of the Havasupai Tribe in Arizona for diabetes research were later used without consent for studies of schizophrenia, inbreeding and migration origins; Arizona State University settled, paying compensation and returning samples. It shows that consent applies to specific uses; using data for purposes participants did not agree to – especially research contradicting their origin stories – causes real harm.

Link: it shows that consent applies to specific uses; using data for purposes participants did not agree to – especially research contradicting their origin stories – causes real harm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of informed consent.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Human Terrain System (2007–2014) shows dual use and do no harm.
items.answer: Social scientists embedded with US military units in Iraq and Afghanistan gathered cultural information for commanders. Information given to the military could be used to target people, and consent was compromised in a war zone; the AAA judged participation incompatible with its ethics.

items.stem: Using the Benin Bronzes as an example, explain colonial power and the ethics of representation.
items.answer: Thousands of brass and ivory works were looted from Benin City by a British punitive expedition in 1897 and dispersed to European museums; several institutions began returning them in the 2020s. Museum displays long presented the objects as "primitive art" divorced from the violence of their acquisition; repatriation debates show communities reclaiming control over their heritage.

items.stem: Briefly describe Bourgois's fieldwork with crack dealers in East Harlem and explain what it reveals about competing ethical obligations.
items.answer: Bourgois witnessed illegal acts and violence, changed names and details, and reflected on the risk that his descriptions might reinforce negative stereotypes of Puerto Ricans. He had to protect participants from legal harm while still describing violence honestly, and to avoid representations that could harm the wider community.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that it is impossible to represent another people fairly? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Perfect fairness is unattainable, but collaborative and reflexive methods can make representation more accountable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: the writer's authority and selection always shape the account (Writing Culture); audiences may read texts through stereotypes; collaboration, reflexivity and multiple voices improve fairness; insider and Indigenous anthropologists challenge outsider representations. Suitable ethnographies include Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People, Bourgois's In Search of Respect. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Perfect fairness is unattainable, but collaborative and reflexive methods can make representation more accountable. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Museums should return all objects acquired during the colonial period."
items.answer: Return should be the default where acquisition was coercive, but the form of restitution should be decided with source communities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many were taken by force or under unequal conditions; communities have rights to their heritage and ancestors. Arguments against: some objects were traded or commissioned legitimately; communities may prefer loans, shared stewardship or digital access; decisions should be made with source communities. Supported judgement: Return should be the default where acquisition was coercive, but the form of restitution should be decided with source communities. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The headteacher agreed that I could observe classes at the girls' school and signed the permission letter. In the staffroom, though, Ms Haddad asked me not to write about her lessons: "If the inspectors read that I speak Arabic in the English class, I lose my job." Two pupils showed me a group chat where they share answers before tests and asked if I would "put it in the book". One of them added, laughing, "Use my real name, I want to be famous." When I returned the following term, a new headteacher knew nothing about my research.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a secondary school in Jordan.

Compare the significance of power in the text with its significance in Chagnon's Yanomamö: The Fierce People. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Refer to specific evidence from both the text and the ethnography.
items.answer: Text: Gatekeeper permission does not equal consent from each participant: Ms Haddad withdraws consent for her lessons; pupils are minors and their consent requires guardians; the request to use a real name conflicts with protecting a minor from harm; a new headteacher means consent must be renegotiated. Consent is ongoing and relational. Ethnography – Napoleon Chagnon, Yanomamö: The Fierce People (1968), among Yanomami communities of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil (fieldwork from 1964): Critics argued that the portrayal of the Yanomami as "fierce" was used by gold miners and politicians to justify encroachment on Yanomami land. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every evening, Nadia brings me tea and asks about visas. She knows I have a British passport, and her son wants to study in London. At first I answered vaguely; then I helped him complete an online application. Since then, Nadia introduces me to neighbours as "the one who helps with papers", and three families have asked me for the same help. When I wrote about a dispute between Nadia and her brother over the family land, she asked to read my notes. I hesitated: her brother had told me his side in confidence.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood in Amman, Jordan, during research with Syrian refugee families.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Refugees are vulnerable: do no harm, avoid raising false hopes about visas, keep the brother's confidence, explain clearly the limits of the researcher's role, protect identities of families with uncertain legal status, and consider sharing findings in ways that do not expose internal disputes. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
